title: A car for every Indian family
hook: A failed car company, no car experts, and a huge goal. Can you build India's first family car?

profit.label: Sales
profit.hint: Cars made and money coming in today

future.label: Future
future.hint: How strong Maruti will be in the years ahead

intro.text: Gurgaon, 1981. Ten years ago, a company on this land promised Indians a small car of their own, but it made only a handful of cars before it was shut down. Now the government is trying again with a new company, Maruti Udyog, and it has put you in charge.

s_goal.text: Your goal is 1 lakh cars a year, while all of India buys fewer than 40,000, nearly all of them big, old Ambassadors and Padminis. Nobody on your team has ever built a car, so first you need a foreign carmaker that can show you how.

d1.title: Find a partner
d1.setup: Fiat, Volkswagen, Renault, Peugeot and Nissan have all said no, and most other carmakers want to send their own people to run the plant. Daihatsu of Japan has been your best hope for months, but now a telex shows it plans to build its car with another Indian firm. A few days later, a telex arrives from Suzuki, a smaller Japanese maker. It wants in.
d1.question: Who do you build India's car with?
d1.advisor: The last Maruti made promises and no cars, so we cannot move slowly. But this partner will shape the company for years.

options.label: Keep working on Daihatsu. The talks are far along, while Suzuki is still a stranger.
options.outcome: You push Daihatsu for months, and late in the year it finally signs. But India is a side project for it, so it sends only a small team, and you are behind before the first machine arrives.
options.why: Daihatsu had already shown it wasn't keen. A partner that doesn't care gives you its spare time, not its best people, and you lost months finding that out.
options.better: Go with the partner that comes to you hungry, even if it is smaller and less famous.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you waited on a partner that had stopped caring.

options.label: Open talks with Suzuki. It is smaller and unfamiliar, but it came to you.
options.outcome: Talks begin in April 1982. Suzuki's president meets your team himself, and his money offer is the best you get. On 2 October 1982 you sign, and Suzuki buys about a quarter of Maruti, with a plan to own more later.
options.why: Suzuki wanted this deal more than anyone, so you got its boss's time and its best terms. An eager partner can teach you more than a famous one that doesn't care.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you picked the hungry partner over the famous one.

options.label: Sign with a maker that will run the plant itself and get a car out faster.
options.outcome: A foreign maker signs quickly and flies in its own managers and machines. Work starts fast, but your Indian staff are kept at the side, watching, while every big decision is made far away.
options.why: Maruti was meant to teach India to build cars. When a partner runs everything, you end up with a factory but none of the know-how.
options.better: Pick a partner that will train your own people and help Indian suppliers grow.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you bought a factory instead of learning to build one.

d2.title: Which car first?

setup.text: Suzuki makes three vehicles you could build: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly inside cities. But Indian families are big, and a van seats more.

Daihatsu makes three vehicles you could build: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly inside cities. But Indian families are big, and a van seats more.

Your partner offers three vehicles you could build: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly inside cities. But Indian families are big, and a van seats more.

d2.question: Which one do you build first?
d2.advisor: A van can carry a whole family or a shop's goods, and the army and police will buy jeeps. The small car is the cheapest, but will Indians trust a car that small?

options.label: Build the jeep. The army, the police and government offices could buy it in bulk.
options.outcome: Government offices place big orders before the first jeep is even built. But to most Indians, Maruti now looks like one more maker of vehicles for officials, and families still have no car they can afford.
options.why: A safe bulk buyer is tempting, but Maruti was set up to put families on wheels. Jeeps for officials served the few, not the many.
options.better: Start with the small family car. A jeep can come later.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you built for officials, not for families.

options.label: Build the van. It fits a big family, and shops can carry goods in it.
options.outcome: Shopkeepers and taxi owners like the van, and it sells. But a family on a scooter still can't buy a car, and that was the reason Maruti was started.
options.why: A van was useful, but India's biggest gap was a car that a middle-class family could afford.
options.better: Build the small car first, and add the van soon after.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you started with a useful van, but missed the biggest need.

options.label: Build the small car. It is the cheapest to buy and run, but it is tiny.

outcome.text: You pick a car based on Suzuki's 1979 Alto, with a small 796 cc engine. You will call it the Maruti 800. For Indian buyers almost everything about it is new, from front-wheel drive and disc brakes to a gear lever on the floor.
Your partner's small car is light and cheap to run, which is just what city families need, although it will take work to make it ready for Indian roads.

options.why: You built for the way Indians really travelled: small groups, short city trips and tight budgets. The car was small enough to be cheap and big enough for four.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you built the car most families could use and afford.

text.text: The launch is set for December 1983. In just 14 months you must build a factory, find hundreds of Indian firms to make parts, and sign up dealers across the country. Your people fly to Japan to learn how Suzuki does it.
The launch is set for December 1983, and Daihatsu's slow start has eaten into your time. You still need a factory, hundreds of Indian firms to make parts, and dealers across the country.
The launch is set for December 1983. Your partner's managers are building the factory fast, and they want to bring almost every part from abroad. You still need dealers across the country.

d3.title: Make the date
d3.setup: The Indian parts makers are not ready. Their quality is uneven and their parts often arrive late. If you wait for them, there will be no car in December.
d3.question: How do you make the launch date?
d3.advisor: If we miss the date, people will say Maruti has failed again. But if everything comes from abroad, how Indian is our car?

options.label: Launch with imported parts, and promise to make the car Indian within five years.

outcome.text: Your workers put together kits shipped from Japan. When the first 192 cars roll out in December 1983, the only Indian parts are the MRF tyres and the Chloride batteries, so less than 3% of the car is Indian. You promise to reach 95% within five years.
You put together parts shipped by your partner and make the date. Very little of the car is Indian yet, but you now have a plan to change that.

options.why: You kept the launch date with imported parts, and you bound yourself to a clear plan for building up Indian suppliers.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you launched on time and made a firm plan to go local.

options.label: Delay the launch until Indian parts makers can do the job properly.
options.outcome: December comes and goes with no car. The papers start calling Maruti another failed dream, and Delhi starts asking hard questions.
options.why: Building local was the right goal, but missing the date cost you trust and time that you could not get back.
options.better: Launch on time with imported parts, and set firm dates for switching to Indian ones.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you put a perfect car ahead of an on-time car.

options.label: Use today's Indian parts as they are. You make the date, and it's Indian from day one.
options.outcome: You make the date with an all-Indian vehicle. But within weeks, buyers are back at the dealers with leaks, rattles and breakdowns, and they say the new Maruti is no better than the old cars.
options.why: A new car built from old-quality parts ruins the first impression, and a first impression is very hard to fix.
options.better: Use proven imported parts at first, and raise Indian suppliers to the new standard step by step.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you chose a local label over real quality.

text.text: 14 December 1983, New Delhi. The Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi, hands the keys of the first Maruti 800 to its owner, an Indian Airlines employee who paid Rs 47,500. The plant, the suppliers and the dealers were all built in 14 months.
Your first vehicles rolled out on time in December 1983, but the repair bills are growing, and so are the jokes about Maruti.
December 1983. Your first vehicle rolls out of Gurgaon on time, with the press watching. Now you will find out how many people want one.

s_launch_late.text: Late 1984. Almost a year behind plan, your first vehicle finally rolls out of Gurgaon, and this one is mostly Indian. People are glad to see it, but many of them had stopped believing it would ever come.

d4.title: Price and the queue

setup.text: About 1,20,000 people have booked a car, but in your first year you can make only about 20,000. Some buyers would pay far more than your price to get one sooner. Making more needs foreign money for machines, and India has very little to spare.

Even with the complaints, bookings keep coming, because there is nothing else new to buy. You can't make enough, and some buyers would pay far more than your price to get one sooner. Making more needs foreign money, and India has very little to spare.

Far more buyers have booked than you can supply this year, and some of them would pay well above your price to get one sooner. Making more needs foreign money for machines, and India has very little to spare.

d4.question: What do you do about the price and the queue?
d4.advisor: If we don't take the extra money, middlemen will. But if the price climbs too high, who is this car really for?

options.label: Raise the price to what buyers will pay, and use the money to build more.
options.outcome: Money pours in, but now the clerks and teachers it was made for can't afford it. The papers call it a rich man's toy, and Delhi is not pleased.
options.why: Maruti's promise was a vehicle for ordinary families. Pricing them out broke that promise and turned the government, which owns you, against you.
options.better: Keep the price fair, and find a way to make more, sooner.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you took the quick money and lost the people's trust.

options.label: Keep the price near Rs 50,000 and make buyers wait their turn, even if it takes years.

outcome.text: You hold the price at about Rs 50,000, and buyers wait their turn. But you can make only about 20,000 a year, so the wait grows to almost three years, and some buyers pay middlemen a big extra sum to skip the line.
The fair price wins respect. But the queue grows longer every year, and middlemen start selling places in it.

options.why: The fair price kept faith with families. But there were far too few cars, so the extra money went to middlemen instead of paying for new machines.
options.better: Keep the price fair, and push early for foreign money to build a second line.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you kept the price fair, but the long queue fed the black market.

options.label: Keep the price and ask Delhi for a foreign loan. Delhi rarely says yes, and it takes time.
options.outcome: It takes months of meetings, but Delhi agrees and a foreign loan comes through. A second line starts years early, the wait gets shorter, and the middlemen lose their business.
options.why: You kept the price fair and went after the real problem, which was too few cars.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you kept the price fair and fixed supply instead of rationing it.

d5.title: Build Indian suppliers

setup.text: Until March 1984, less than a tenth of each car is made in India, and every imported part costs foreign money. To keep your promise, hundreds of small Indian firms must learn to make much better parts. Then a powerful politician asks to become one of your suppliers himself.

Your partner's managers want to keep buying from their own suppliers abroad, and every imported part costs foreign money. Hundreds of Indian firms are waiting for a chance. Then a powerful politician asks to become one of your suppliers himself.

Your Indian suppliers are making parts now, but their quality is uneven, and hundreds of them must learn to work to a higher standard. Then a powerful politician asks to become one of your suppliers himself.

Too many parts still come from abroad, and every one costs foreign money. Hundreds of Indian firms must learn to work to a higher standard. Then a powerful politician asks to become one of your suppliers himself.

d5.question: How do you choose your suppliers?
d5.advisor: Our car is only as good as its worst bolt. And in Delhi, someone is watching every order we give.

options.label: Make him a supplier. The government owns Maruti, and you may need Delhi later.
options.outcome: The politician is pleased. But his parts are poor, cars come back for repairs, and good suppliers stop bidding for your work because they think the game is fixed.
options.why: Once connections beat quality, good suppliers give up, and your car gets worse.
options.better: Pick suppliers on quality alone, and say no to pressure politely but firmly.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you traded quality for favours.

options.label: Pick suppliers on quality alone and train them. It's slow, and the politician will be angry.

outcome.text: Your supplier team tells him to bring a sample and be tested like everyone else, and he never comes back. Hundreds of firms have to change their machines, their methods and their habits, and once it is clear that Maruti will not fail, they take it seriously. In 1984–85 you beat your target of 20,000 cars.
You tell the politician he will be tested like everyone else, and you hold every supplier to one standard. It is slow and painful, but parts start arriving on time and fitting right.

options.why: You built a supplier base on merit and helped it grow, which made the car cheaper, more Indian and better, all at once.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you chose suppliers on quality, not connections, and helped them grow.

options.label: Keep buying most parts abroad for now. Quality stays safe, but foreign money keeps leaving.
options.outcome: Quality stays high, but each car eats up scarce foreign money, Delhi grows impatient, and Indian suppliers never get their chance to grow.
options.why: Imports were safe, but they kept costs high, drained foreign money and broke your promise to go local.
options.better: Choose Indian suppliers on quality alone and help them improve, so the car becomes Indian step by step.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you played safe with imports and built no local strength.

text.text: It is 1987, and Maruti is growing up fast. A van joined the 800 in 1984 and the Gypsy jeep came in 1985. In 1986 the 1,00,000th Maruti rolled out, and the 800 got a newer body. Yet the queue at home is still years long.
It is 1987. Your vehicles are on Indian roads, but so are the stories about weak parts, and the best suppliers now work for other companies.
It is 1987. Your vehicles sell well to people with money, but most families still ride scooters, and the papers have not forgotten your price rise.
It is 1987. The second line is running, and the wait for a Maruti is shrinking. Many families who booked in 1984 already have theirs.
It is 1987. Your vehicles are on Indian roads, and people are still queuing for them. Now you have to decide how far to push Maruti.

d6.title: Sell abroad?

setup.text: Buyers at home are still queuing, so you could sell every car you make in India. Suzuki and your own chairman both say you should not try to sell abroad.
Buyers at home are still queuing, so you could sell everything you make in India. Your partner and your own chairman both say you should not try to sell abroad.

d6.question: What do you do next?
d6.advisor: Europe is far away, and we have never sold a car there. But at home, nobody is pushing us to get better.

options.label: Sell some cars in Europe, against the advice of your partner and your chairman.

outcome.text: You ship 500 cars to Hungary, and the first ones arrive on 24 October 1987. France follows in 1989 and the Netherlands in 1990. To sell in Europe, the 800 gets seat belts, which it never had before.
Selling abroad pushes your plant and your suppliers toward world standards, and buyers in other countries start to notice your vehicles.

options.why: With no rivals at home, you used tough foreign buyers to keep raising your standards.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you went abroad to get better, not just bigger.

options.label: Stay in India. Every car you make already sells, and your partner agrees.
options.outcome: Sales stay strong. But with no tough buyers to answer to, quality improves slowly, and when rivals arrive years later, you are less ready than you should be.
options.why: It was safe, but a company with no competition needs another way to keep getting better.
options.better: Sell some cars abroad to learn from tougher buyers, even while the queue at home is long.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you stayed home and missed a chance to raise your game.

options.label: Speed up the line and cut some checks, so more people get cars sooner.
options.outcome: More cars leave the gate, and more come back broken. Buyers start saying that Maruti is just like the old car makers.
options.why: You used the queue as an excuse to drop your standards, which were the very thing that made Maruti different.
options.better: Test yourself against tougher buyers, so quality keeps rising even with no rivals at home.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you let the queue lower your standards.

text.text: By 1988 Gurgaon can make 1,00,000 cars a year, the goal you were given in 1981. The 800 stays on sale until 2014, and nearly 29 lakh are built. In 2024, about 4 in every 10 cars sold in India are still Marutis.
Because you built a second line early, the queue ends years sooner, and Indian suppliers grow with you. For millions of families, a Maruti becomes their first car.
You built the people's car and a strong group of Indian suppliers around it. For millions of families, a Maruti becomes their first car.

survivor.title: A good company, a smaller dream

text.text: Maruti makes good jeeps and good money, mostly from government orders. But it never becomes the family car of India, and when foreign rivals arrive in the 1990s, they take that prize.
Maruti's vans are everywhere, carrying goods and families. But the small family car comes late, and when foreign rivals arrive in the 1990s, Maruti is a strong player, not the clear leader.
Maruti makes good cars and good money, but it never becomes the car of every Indian family. When foreign rivals arrive in the 1990s, it is a strong player, not the clear leader.

collapse.title: Another failed dream
collapse.text: The vehicles cost too much or break too often, and Indian suppliers never grow. Like the first Maruti, the company becomes the story of a big promise that did not come true.

fired.title: Delhi lets you go
fired.text: Delhi has seen enough. After three costly calls, the government, which owns Maruti, gives your job to someone else, and the people's car must wait for a new boss.

realHistory: In 1981 the government started Maruti Udyog, a company with no car experience. In October 1982 it signed with Suzuki, a late but eager partner, and in just 14 months it built a factory in Gurgaon, a group of suppliers and a dealer network. The first Maruti 800 was handed over on 14 December 1983. About 1,20,000 people booked in the first year, far more than Maruti could make. Maruti pushed hundreds of Indian suppliers to raise their quality, began exporting to Europe in 1987, and could make 1,00,000 cars a year by 1988. The 800 stayed on sale until 2014, and Maruti Suzuki is still India's biggest carmaker.
